parole.significato: A tax paid for building or repairing the walls of a fortified town.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English murage, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French murage, from murer (“to wall”), from mur (“wall”), Latin murus. See mure (“wall”).

parole.testo: The noun is derived from Late Middle English morein, morine, moreyn (“(widespread) death; widespread sickness, plague; fatal disease; carnage; carrion”), from Anglo-Norman morine, mourine, moreyn (“death; widespread sickness, plague; carrion; cattle disease”), Middle French morine, and Old French mo

parole.significato: A gathering.
parole.testo: From Middle English musteren, borrowed from Anglo-Norman mostrer, Middle French monstrer, moustrer (whence the noun monstre, which gave the English noun), from Latin mōnstrō (“to show”), from moneō (“to admonish”). Cognate with French montrer (“to show”), Italian mostrare (“to show”), Spanish mostra

parole.significato: Not having the power of speech; dumb.
parole.testo: From Middle English muet, from Anglo-Norman muet, moet, Middle French muet, from mu (“dumb, mute”) + -et, remodelled after Latin mūtus.

parole.significato: Household linen, especially table linen.
parole.testo: From Middle English naperie, from Anglo-Norman naperie, Middle French naperie, from Old French nape + -erie.

parole.significato: Someone's birth; the place, time and circumstances of a birth.
parole.testo: From Middle English nativite, from Anglo-Norman nativite, Middle French nativite, and their source, Latin nātīvitās (“birth”). By surface analysis, native + -ity. See also naïveté.

parole.significato: A kind of hymn, or canticle, of mediaeval origin, sung in honor of the birth of Christ; a Christmas carol.
parole.testo: From Middle English nowel, from Anglo-Norman noel, Middle French noel, a variant of nael, from Latin adjective nātālis (“natal, having to do with birth”).

parole.significato: A beginner; one who is not very familiar or experienced in a particular subject.
parole.testo: From Middle English novice, novys, from Anglo-Norman novice, Middle French novice, itself borrowed from Latin novīcius, later novitius (“new, newly arrived”) (in Late Latin as a noun, masculine novicius, feminine novicia (“one who has newly entered a monastery or a convent”)), from novus (“new”).

parole.significato: The death of a person.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman obit, Middle French obit, and their source, Latin obitus (“going down; death”), from obīre (“to go down, to die”).

parole.significato: To get hold of; to gain possession of, to procure; to acquire, in any way.
parole.testo: From Middle English obteinen, from Anglo-Norman obtenir, optiner et al., and Middle French obtenir, from Latin obtinēre (“to gain, achieve, succeed, possess”), from ob- + tenēre (“to hold”).

parole.significato: The Asiatic wild ass or hemione (Equus hemionus), an animal of the horse family native to Asia; specifically, the Persi…
parole.testo: From Middle English onager, onagir (“wild ass; military catapult”), from Anglo-Norman onager, Middle French onager, onagre, Old French onager, onagre (“wild ass; military catapult”) (modern French onagre), from Late Latin onager (“large siege engine”), Latin onager (“wild ass”), from Hellenistic Anc

parole.significato: A belief, judgment or perspective that a person has formed, either through objective or subjective reasoning, about a t…
parole.testo: From English opine + -ion, from Middle English opinion, opinioun, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French opinion, from Latin opīniō, from opīnor (“to opine”). Displaced native Old English wēna.

parole.significato: A private chapel or prayer room.
parole.testo: From Middle English oratorie, from Anglo-Norman oratorie, Middle French oratoire, and their source, Late Latin ōrātōrium. Doublet of oratorio. Displaced native Old English bēdhūs.

parole.significato: Having regular jurisdiction; now only used in certain phrases.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman ordenarie, ordenaire et al., Middle French ordinaire, and their source, Medieval Latin ordinarius, noun use of Latin ōrdinārius (“regular, orderly”), from ōrdō (“order”).

parole.significato: Of a pearl or other precious stone: having a superior lustre.
parole.testo: From Middle English oriental, from Anglo-Norman oriental, Middle French oriental, from Latin orientālis (“eastern”), from oriēns (“rising (of the Sun)”), present active participle of orior (“to rise”).

parole.significato: Any elaborate embroidery, especially when made of gold thread; an object (such as clothing or fabric) adorned with such…
parole.testo: From Middle English orfray, orfrei, orefreys (“elaborate (especially gold) embroidery; fabric adorned with such embroidery; embroidered ornamental band or border; decorative elements”), from Anglo-Norman and Middle French orfrais, orfreis, orfrois, and other forms, from Late Latin aurifrasium, aurif

parole.significato: Violating morality or decency; provoking indignation or affront.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman outrageus, Middle French outrageus, from outrage; equivalent to outrage + -ous.

parole.significato: That which remains beyond what is necessary or required; a surplus.
parole.testo: From over- + Anglo-Norman plus, Middle French plus.

parole.significato: Open and not concealed or secret.
parole.testo: From Middle English overt, uverte (“open, uncovered; unfastened; accessible, unobstructed; clear, manifest”), from Anglo-Norman overt, Middle French ouvert, Old French overt, ouvert, uvert (“opened”) (modern French ouvert), past participle of Anglo-Norman, Old French ovrir, ouvrir, uvrir (“to open”)

parole.significato: An opening; a recess or chamber.
parole.testo: From Middle English overture, from Anglo-Norman, Middle French overture, from Old French overture, from Latin apertūra. Doublet of aperture.

parole.significato: A type of elaborate robe especially as worn by someone in power or a religious official.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman parement, Middle French parement, from Medieval Latin parāmentum, from parō (“adorn”) + -mentum.

parole.significato: A person who raises a child (which they have made, adopted, fostered, taken as their own, etc.).
parole.testo: From Middle English parent, borrowed from Anglo-Norman parent, Middle French parent, from Latin parentem, accusative of parēns (“parent”), present participle of pariō (“to breed, bring forth”).

parole.significato: Pertaining only to a part of something; partial.
parole.testo: From Middle English particuler, from Anglo-Norman particuler, Middle French particuler, particulier, from Late Latin particularis (“partial; separate, individual”), from Latin particula (“(small) part”). Equivalent to particle + -ar. Compare particle.

parole.significato: Conspicuous; open; unconcealed.
parole.testo: From Middle English patent, patente (“wide open; clear, unobstructed; unlimited; of a document: available for public inspection”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman and Middle French patent (modern French patent), and directly from their etymon Latin patēns (“open; accessible, passable; evident, m

parole.significato: A paved surface; a hard covering on the ground.
parole.testo: From Middle English pament, from Anglo-Norman pavement and reinforced by Middle French pavement; both from Latin pavīmentum (“paved surface or floor”), from pavīre (“to beat, to ram, to tread down”). Morphologically pave + -ment.

parole.significato: Favouring peace rather than conflict; not aggressive, tending to avoid violence (of people, actions etc.).
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pesible, peisible, Middle French paisible, from pais (“peace”) + -ible; later remodelled after peace + -able.

parole.significato: A type of pear.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman parmain, peremain et al., Middle French parmain, permain (“type of pear or apple”), of uncertain origin.

parole.significato: Pecuniary.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pecunier, Middle French pécunier, alteration of pecuniaire, from Latin pecūniārius.

parole.significato: To weigh or measure the weight of; to poise.
parole.testo: From Middle English peysen, from Anglo-Norman peiser, peser and Middle French peser, from Latin pēnsāre (literally “weigh”). Doublet of poise.

parole.significato: A supporting post attached to the main rafter.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pendaunt, Middle French pendant, noun use of adjective.

parole.testo: From Late Middle English pennon, penoun (“long narrow flag attached to a lance or used in other contexts; one who bears a pennon, knight bachelor; plume of feathers; strip around the edge of a shield”), from Anglo-Norman penun (“feather of an arrow”), penoun (“flag attached to a lance”), Middle Fren

parole.significato: A transparent olive green form of olivine, used as a gem.
parole.testo: From Middle English peritot, from Anglo-Norman peridou, peridout, Middle French perido, peridon, of uncertain origin; later reborrowed from modern French péridot.

parole.significato: Having little or no importance.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Middle English peti, pety (“little, small; minor”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman petit, Middle French petit, and Old French peti, petit, pitet (“young; little, small; inferior; insignificant”) (modern French petit), ultimately of imitative origin. parole.significato: A lover of wisdom.
parole.testo: From Middle English philosophre, from Anglo-Norman or Middle French philosophe, from Latin philosophus, from Ancient Greek φιλόσοφος (philósophos, literally “lover of wisdom”) + -er. Credited as having been coined by Pythagoras to describe himself. Displaced native Old English ūþwita.

parole.significato: A plant of the genus Pimpinella, especially burnet saxifrage (Pimpinella saxifraga).

parole.significato: Flat, level.
parole.testo: From Middle English pleyn, borrowed from Anglo-Norman pleyn, playn, Middle French plain, plein, and Old French plain, from Latin plānus (“flat, even, level, plain”). Doublet of llano, piano, plane, and plan.

parole.significato: A plot of land; a lot.

parole.significato: Fullness; completeness.
parole.testo: From Middle English plenitude, that borrowed from Anglo-Norman plenitude, Middle French plenitude, and their source, Latin plēnitūdō.

parole.significato: A state of balance, equilibrium or stability.

parole.significato: A statement made on oath by a jury.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman presentment, presentement, Middle French presentement, corresponding to present + -ment.

parole.significato: A region or sovereign nation headed by a prince or princess.
parole.testo: From Middle English principalte, principalite, from Anglo-Norman principalté, Middle French principalté, from Late Latin prīncipālitās, from Latin prīncipālis (“principal”) + -tās. Equivalent to principal + -ity.

parole.significato: A forefather, any of a person's direct ancestors.
parole.testo: From Middle English progenitour, from Anglo-Norman progenitour, Middle French progeniteur (Modern French progéniteur), and their etymon Latin prōgenitor, from prōgenitus, perfect participle of prōgignere (“to beget”), itself from prō- (“forth”) + gignere (“to beget”). parole.significato: The act of propitiating; placation, atonement, similar to expiation but also involving the appeasement of anger.

parole.significato: To suggest a plan, course of action, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle English proposen, from Anglo-Norman proposer (verb), propos (noun), Middle French proposer (verb), propos (noun), from Latin prōpōnō, prōpōnere, with conjugation altered based on poser. Doublet of propound.

parole.significato: The particular character or essence of someone or something; individuality.
parole.testo: From late Middle English proprietee, propretee, propriete (“ownership”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman propreté, Middle French proprieté, from Latin proprietās. By surface analysis, prop(e)r + -iety. Doublet of property.

parole.significato: Causing something to last longer or remain in effect longer; prolongation, continuance.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman prorogation, Middle French prorogation, and their source, Latin prōrogātiō (“extension, postponement”).

parole.significato: Preparation for the future; good governance; foresight.
parole.testo: From Middle English providence, from Anglo-Norman providence, Middle French providence, and their source, Latin prōvidentia (“providence, foresight”), from the present participle of prōvidēre (“to provide”). By surface analysis, provide + -ence. Displaced native Old English foresċēawung.

parole.significato: A girl, a maiden; a virgin (often with reference to Joan of Arc).
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman pucele, Middle French pucele, perhaps from a Late Latin *pullicella, but the further etymology is disputed. Compare Sicilian pulla.

parole.significato: A dispute or heated argument (especially one that is verbal).
parole.testo: From Middle English querele (“altercation, dispute; argument, debate; armed combat; trial by combat; basis for dispute, complaint; claim, legal suit; a lament; illness”) [and other forms], from Anglo-Norman querele [and other forms] and Middle French querele, querelle (“altercation, dispute; basis f

parole.significato: An object (generally a post or plank on a support) set up as a target to be tilted at in jousting, or otherwise used as…
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman quintaine, quinteine, Middle French quintaine, probably from Latin quīntāna (“street separating fifth and sixth maniples in a Roman camp”), feminine form of quīntānus (“pertaining to the fifth”).

parole.significato: Synonym of hundredweight, 100 or 112 English or American pounds.

parole.significato: Happening every day; daily.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman cotidian, cotidien, Middle French cotidian, cotidien, and their source, Latin cottīdiānus, quōtīdiānus (“happening every day”), from adverb cottīdiē, quōtīdiē (“every day, daily”), from an unattested adjective derived from quot (“how many”) + locative form of diēs (“day”).

parole.significato: To gush; to flow.
parole.testo: Probably from Anglo-Norman raier, Middle French raier.

parole.significato: A type of fine linen once imported from France.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman Reins, Middle French Reins, variant of Reims, the French town where the fabric was originally produced.

parole.significato: To hack, slash, or slice (something).
parole.testo: Probably a variant of race, raze (“to demolish; to destroy, obliterate; to scrape as if with a razor”), possibly modelled after rash (etymology 5 or etymology 6). parole.significato: Scraping the surface of a parchment etc. in order to erase something from the document; erasure, more generally.
parole.testo: From Middle English rasure, from Anglo-Norman rasure, Middle French rasure, from Latin rāsūra (“scraping, shaving”), from the participle stem of rādō (“to scrape, shave”).

parole.significato: A rat.
parole.testo: From Middle English ratoun, from Anglo-Norman ratoun and Middle French raton, corresponding to rat + -oon.

parole.significato: The rearmost part of a force, especially a detachment of troops that protect the rear of a retreating force.
parole.testo: From Middle English rier garde, from Anglo-Norman reregard, reregarde, rereguarde and Middle French rieregarde, from Old French rereguarde (attested in The Song of Roland, c. 1150), from rere (“after; behind”) + guarde (“guard”). By surface analysis, rear + guard. Piecewise doublet of retrogarde.

parole.significato: A subsequent brief recitement or enumeration of the major points in a narrative, article, or book.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman recapitulaciun et al., Middle French recapitulacion et al., or their source, from Late Latin recapitulatio (“summing up, summary”), from the participle stem of recapitulare (“recapitulate”), from re- + capitulum (“chapter, section”), diminutive of caput (“head”).

parole.significato: A container.
parole.testo: From Middle English receptacle, from Anglo-Norman receptacle and Middle French receptacle (“organ containing a fluid; gathering place; water basin”) (modern French réceptacle), from Latin receptāculum (“animal enclosure, container, place of refuge, receptacle, repository, reservoir, shelter”), from

parole.significato: To return land to a suitable condition for use.
parole.testo: From Middle English reclaymen, recleymen, reclamen, from Anglo-Norman reclamer (noun reclaim and Middle French reclamer (noun reclaim), from Latin reclāmō, reclāmāre. Equivalent to re- + claim.

parole.significato: To console (someone); to comfort, look after.
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman reconforter, Middle French reconforter, from re- + conforter.

parole.significato: Having admitted defeat and surrendered; defeated.
parole.testo: From Middle English recreaunt, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French recreant (“defeated”), from recroire (“to yield in a trial by combat, surrender allegiance”). Compare miscreant.

parole.significato: Especially of a person.

parole.significato: To swell up (of water, waves etc.); to overflow, to surge (of bodily fluids).
parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman redunder, Middle French redonder, and their source, Latin redundō, from red- + undō (“surge”), from unda (“a wave”).

parole.significato: To put in order again; to set right; to revise.
parole.testo: From Middle English redressen, from Anglo-Norman radresser, redrescer, redrescier and Middle French redresser (“to stand (someone or something) up; to stand up again; to rebuild, to repair something damaged, to rectify, to restore; to obtain redress; to cure; (of hair) to stand on end; to revise a j

parole.significato: With the head turned toward the back of the body.
parole.testo: From Middle English regardant, from Anglo-Norman regardant, Middle French regardant.

parole.significato: One who rules in place of the monarch, especially because the monarch is too young, absent, or disabled.
parole.testo: From Middle English regent, from Anglo-Norman regent, Middle French regent, and their source, Latin regēns (“ruling; ruler, governor, prince”), present participle of regō (“to govern, to steer”).

parole.significato: Bound by religious rule; belonging to a monastic or religious order (often as opposed to secular).

parole.significato: A kidney.

parole.testo: From Middle English seignurie, from Anglo-Norman seignurie, Middle French signeurie, signerie et al., later influenced by Italian signoria. Compare seigniory.

parole.significato: Truth, fact or reality, especially an enduring religious or ethical truth; veracity.
parole.testo: From Middle English verite, from Anglo-Norman verité or Middle French verité, from Old French verité, from Latin vēritās, from the adjective vērus (“true”). Doublet of veritas.

parole.testo: From Anglo-Norman vicontiel, from Middle French visconte (“viscount”) + -iel. Equivalent to viscount + -ial.
